newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish bonds to take breather after steep rally.
newsitem.headline: Spanish bonds to take breather after steep rally.

text.p: In the next two weeks Spanish bonds are expecting a lot of good news -- a tight budget and a cut in official rates -- but analysts believe that bond prices have over-indulged and the celebration is almost over.

In less than a month, the prices of Spanish bonds have risen almost 400 basis points and the ten year yield has fallen 50 basis points to under 8.10 percent on Friday from around 8.60 percent when September started.

"The market is discounting too many factors and too fast," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid. "I am positive over a nine months period, but for the next two or three weeks it seems to me the party is over."
The 10-year spread over German Bunds dipped on Friday under the resistance level of 200, while the differential over Italian Btp stood around 90 basis points.
"What we have here is a global shift toward non-core countries, a general re-weighting in investors portfolios," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist with Societe Generale in Madrid.
"In the coming days a correction is possible," he said. "A spread of less than 200 basis points over Germany before the 1997 budget draft is presented is a little bit scary."

At 1500 GMT the December future contract on Meff was trading 90 basis points over yesterday's close at 105.40 after hitting a record high at 105.70. The 10-year yield on the cash market is at 8.07 percent, while the spread over German Bunds is 196.

The main factor supporting the Bono market is the growing conviction that Spain can be at the starting block of the European Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999. And some economists point out that Spain is better off than Italy, at least on paper.
"The market seems convinced Spain can join EMU in 1999, before and without Italy," Lumholdt said.
"I do not believe this is going to happen since Italy is a Group of Seven country and the other European partners can't include Spain and leave Italy out".
Dealers are also increasingly optimistic on Spain's chances to reduce inflation after tamer than expected August inflation of 3.7 percent.
"We believe Spanish inflation can be 3.3/3.4 percent by year-end," said one economist.

"The government's attitude seems to be an anti-inflationary one," said Carmen Alcaide, economist with BBV in Madrid, who expects the Spanish inflation rate to go under three percent level sometime next spring.
The government confirmed on Thursday that it would freeze public sector salaries in 1997.
Declining inflation should pave the way for a fresh rate cut from the Bank of Spain, which many dealers expect on October 3, the date of the first repo tender after the 1997 budget presentation.

"The market is discounting a cut of between 25 and 50 basis points," a dealer explained. "I think a 25 basis point cut is already there, while a 50 basis point cut will depend on how austere the budget is judged," Urrutia said.

"The yield curve is almost flat: overnight rates are at 7.25 percent while five-year bonds are yielding 7.30 percent" a dealer said. "Either short term interest rates have to go down or the long-end has to go up".
